content: Efforts to support and influence discussions on funding allocations across the water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) sector have proven effective over the years. WASH accounts have become a critical tool for raising awareness among decision-makers about funding gaps in the sector and advocating for progressive increases in financial support. For example, in Mali, improved knowledge of sector financing has led to increased funding allocations. This progress is supported by initiatives such as the TrackFin project, which tracked financing for drinking water, sanitation, and hygiene services between 2012 and 2014. In Ghana, the Asutifi North District Assembly initiated a collaborative effort in 2018 to address challenges in reaching underserved populations and improving service levels in rural areas and small towns. This effort involved local and national government leaders, community chiefs, women, water service providers, private sector representatives, NGOs, and implementation partners. A comprehensive assessment of WASH services was conducted, leading to the development of a district WASH master plan. This plan outlined steps to achieve universal and sustainable access to safe water, including a clear vision, mediumand long-term strategies, a costed plan with funding sources, and a monitoring and evaluation framework. Since 2018, annual data collection has been conducted to monitor the plan's implementation, with indicators aligned with Ghana's Community Water and Sanitation Agency framework. This data has informed planning, resource allocation, and actions such as tariff setting and revenue collection, resulting in a doubling of the district WASH budget from 2018 to 2019. In Nepal, the lack of a consolidated management information system for WASH data was addressed in 2018 with the development of the National Water Supply, Sanitation, and Hygiene Management Information System. This system integrates data from urban and rural contexts, covering indicators such as sustainability, functionality, and water quality. The Ministry of Water Supply has made the system accessible to a wide range of stakeholders, enabling evidence-based decision-making for national and subnational plans and programs. In Latin America and Africa, the Rural Water and Sanitation Information System (SIASAR), launched in 2011, has expanded to 15 countries, covering over 5 million rural inhabitants. This system provides a unified platform for monitoring, planning, and evaluating rural water and sanitation services. It harmonizes tools and approaches, enabling data comparison across sites and countries. In Colombia, SIASAR was adopted in 2017 to monitor rural water provision, supporting decisions such as prioritizing water access in Indigenous farming communities and planning water supply construction in underserved municipalities. In Ethiopia, a 2022 water quality assessment in three districts involved collaboration between a local university and an international research institute. Water samples were collected from community water points, schools, healthcare facilities, and household storage containers. The findings were presented to local government actors to prioritize resources for infrastructure development and corrective actions to protect public health. Simplified summaries of results were shared with community members, motivating actions such as fencing water points and requesting water chlorination. In Kenya and Tanzania, regulators produce annual performance reports benchmarking water service providers against key indicators. These reports use visual formats, such as traffic-light color coding, to highlight performance and changes over time. In Kenya, the Water Services Regulatory Board evaluates over 90 providers, including small providers, while Tanzania's Energy and Water Utilities Regulatory Authority produces reports for regional and district-level services. These reports are shared during workshops and award ceremonies to enhance accountability and inform planning and budgeting cycles. In 2018, the Department of Water Resources introduced the National Implementation Plan for Safe and Secure Community Drinking Water, which prioritizes communities for infrastructure upgrades based on systematic reviews of water safety and security plans. Advisory committees at provincial and national levels review these plans to allocate annual budgets effectively. In Myanmar, the Department of Rural Development adopted an electronic system in 2019 to manage rural drinking water services. This system tracks indicators such as water supply functionality, availability, quality, and user payments. It supports asset management and aligns with national targets and Sustainable Development Goal 6. Local government staff regularly update the data, which informs annual planning and budgeting processes for water supply maintenance and expansion. Sanitary inspections (SIs) are a low-cost, rapid risk assessment tool used to identify and manage risks in water supplies. These inspections evaluate physical structures, operations, and environmental factors to detect contamination sources and inadequacies. SIs are particularly valuable for small drinking water supplies with limited resources. They support routine risk management by water suppliers and surveillance agencies, contributing to safe water supply management. The World Health Organization has developed 13 SI packages for common water supply technologies, providing checklists, technical fact sheets, and management advice to guide corrective actions and improve water safety.
